Most Nigerian tailors start with **bespoke** work: the client brings fabric, you take measurements, she pays a deposit and collects later. Bespoke work needs little stock, because the client usually supplies the fabric, but your income depends on your hours. **Ready-to-wear** can grow beyond your own hands because you can sew in batches, but you must buy fabric first and wait for buyers. Many successful small brands mix the two: bespoke work pays the bills while a small RTW line builds the brand.

Know your customer, not just your style

Saying 'I sew for everybody' feels safe but makes marketing hard. A **customer group** (also called a niche) is a group of people with the same need, budget and buying habits. Examples: working women who need corporate gowns and skirt suits; brides and their families buying aso-ebi; men who wear senator and kaftan styles to church and events; mothers buying children's party wear; plus-size women who struggle to find good fits in ready-made clothes.
**Who is she?** Age range, work, where she lives, how she dresses on a normal day.
**What does she buy?** Styles, fabrics (Ankara, lace, aso-oke, adire, plain cotton), how often.
**What does she spend?** A realistic price band per outfit in your area.
**When does she buy?** Christmas and New Year, Easter, Eid (Sallah), wedding seasons, school resumption, end-of-year office parties.
**Where does she look?** WhatsApp status, Instagram, church or mosque groups, word of mouth, a market shop.
Plan for your peak season

Festive periods bring more orders than one person can sew. Decide in advance the date after which you stop accepting orders for that season, and tell clients early. A clear cut-off protects your name better than rushed, late outfits.
Worked example: narrowing the business
For example, Chiamaka runs a two-machine shop in Owerri. She sews anything that walks in: school uniforms, men's trousers, bridal gowns and repairs. She is always busy but rarely has savings.
She looks back over her last 40 orders in her notebook and groups them: 22 women's gowns and skirt suits, 8 men's styles, 6 repairs, 4 bridal pieces.
She notes that the women's office wear came mostly from referrals among bank and school staff, and that these clients paid deposits without long bargaining.
She notes that bridal pieces took about three times longer than a gown and caused the most fitting disputes.
She writes her statement: 'I make well-fitted office and church wear for working women in Owerri, ready in 7 to 10 days.'
She keeps repairs as a small side service but stops accepting bridal gowns until she has trained help.
Chiamaka now has a clear customer to market to, a turnaround time she can promise, and fewer jobs that eat her time. Her marketing can speak directly to working women instead of everybody.
Your one-sentence business statement

Write one sentence using this pattern: **I make [what] for [whom] in [where], [your promise].** The promise should be something you can keep every time, such as a turnaround time, a fit guarantee with one free adjustment, or a finish quality. You will use this sentence in your WhatsApp Business profile, your Instagram bio and when people ask what you do.

Your statement also guides your prices. If you promise fine finishing for working women, you cannot price like a roadside repair stall, and you should not try to. Look at three or four tailors who serve the same customer in your area, note roughly what they charge and how fast they deliver, and decide whether you will compete on speed, finish, fit or style. The most forgotten cost is **your own labour**. If you do not pay yourself for your hours inside the price, you are working for free and calling the leftover money 'profit'. The second most forgotten cost is **overheads**. Fuel for the generator, shop rent and data are real costs of every garment, even though they are paid monthly.
Putting a value on your hour

To include labour, you need an **hourly labour rate**. A simple way: decide what you want to earn as a wage in a normal month, then divide it by the hours you actually sew in that month. For example, if you want about 150,000 naira (approximate) as your own wage and you sew about 150 hours a month (6 hours a day for 25 days), your rate is 150,000 / 150 = 1,000 naira per hour. A gown that takes 8 hours then carries 8,000 naira of labour. If you pay a helper, use what you actually pay her per hour for the work she does. Count only real sewing hours: time spent waiting for light, going to market or chatting with clients belongs in overheads, not in labour.
Margin and markup: two ways to describe profit

**Markup** compares profit with cost. **Margin** compares profit with selling price. They use the same profit but give different percentages, and mixing them up is a common reason tailors undercharge.
Worked example: margin and markup on one gown
For example, Bisi's total cost for a lined Ankara gown is about 30,000 naira (approximate). She sells it for 40,000 naira.
Profit = selling price minus total cost = 40,000 minus 30,000 = 10,000 naira.
Markup = profit divided by cost = 10,000 / 30,000 = 0.333, so about 33%.
Margin = profit divided by selling price = 10,000 / 40,000 = 0.25, so 25%.
If Bisi wants a 25% margin on a garment costing 30,000, she divides cost by (1 minus 0.25): 30,000 / 0.75 = 40,000.
If she wrongly adds 25% to cost (30,000 x 1.25 = 37,500), her margin is only 7,500 / 37,500 = 20%.
The same 10,000 naira profit is a 33% markup but a 25% margin. To hit a target margin, divide cost by (1 minus the margin), do not just add the percentage to cost.
What a price is built from
Overhead share
Materials are the base; labour and overheads sit on top, and profit is only what remains above all three.
The order words
**Deposit:** part payment made before you start, usually enough to cover at least the materials you must buy.
**Balance:** the rest of the price, paid at collection or before delivery.
**Turnaround time:** the number of days from measurement and deposit to a ready garment.
**Order book:** your record of every order: client, style, measurements, price, deposit, balance, due date and status.
**Fitting:** the try-on before final finishing, where you adjust for fit.
**Alteration window:** the period after collection when you will adjust fit at no extra charge.
Sales are not profit

If you collect 500,000 naira from clients in December, that is your **sales** (also called revenue or turnover). It is not your income. Out of it you paid for fabric and lining, paid helpers, bought fuel and paid rent. What remains after all costs is your **profit**. A busy month with poor pricing can bring large sales and very little profit. You will learn to record both in Module 2.
Deposits are not yet yours

A deposit for an order you have not finished is money you still owe in work. If you spend all December deposits on house needs and then cannot buy lining or pay for fuel, the orders fail. Keep deposits for the orders they were paid for until those orders are delivered.

A professional setup does not need a big shop. It needs the right tools in the right place, a legal identity that lets you open a business account and bid for larger jobs, and safety rules that protect you, your helpers and your clients' clothes. This lesson covers all three.
A sewing needle with thread
Good tools, kept in order and kept safe, are the base of a professional workshop.
Workshop tools and organisation
**Machines:** a straight-stitch machine (manual or electric), and ideally an overlock (serger) for clean seam finishes.
**Cutting:** sharp fabric scissors used only on fabric, pinking shears, a seam ripper, tailor's chalk and a cutting table.
**Measuring:** a good tape measure (replace it when it stretches), a metre rule and a hip curve or French curve if you draft patterns.
**Pressing:** an iron and ironing board; pressing during sewing makes a big difference to the finish.
**Storage:** labelled bags or shelves for each client's fabric with her name, order number and due date.
**Records:** an order book or notebook, a receipt book, and a phone with WhatsApp Business.
Label every client's fabric

Lost or mixed-up fabric is one of the most painful disputes in tailoring. The moment a client hands over fabric, tag it with her name, phone number, order number and due date, and photograph it with the tag. That photo is your proof if anything is questioned later.
Registering a business name with CAC

In Nigeria, a business name (for example 'Ada Stitches') is registered with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)** through its online portal. A registered business name lets you open a business bank account in that name, issue proper receipts, and apply for uniform contracts or programmes that ask for registration. It is different from a limited company: a business name does not have a separate legal personality, so the owner remains personally responsible for its debts.
Choose two or more possible names and search for them on the CAC portal; an approved name is reserved for a limited time while you complete registration.
Fill the business name registration form online with the business address, the nature of the business (for example tailoring and fashion design) and the details of each proprietor.
Upload what the portal asks for, such as a means of identification, passport photograph and signature.
Pay the filing fee on the portal (check the current fee on the CAC website or portal at the time).
When approved, download your certificate from your CAC dashboard.
Each year, file the business name's annual return with CAC; late filing attracts penalties.
Avoid registration scams

Use the official CAC website and portal, or an accredited agent you can verify. Do not pay a stranger on social media who promises a certificate 'in one hour'. Keep copies of every payment receipt and your login details private.
Workshop safety

**Electricity:** do not overload one extension socket with the iron, machines and phone chargers; the iron alone draws a lot of power. Use a voltage stabiliser or surge protector for electric machines, and switch off and unplug everything at closing time.
**Generator:** never run a generator indoors, in a passage or near windows. Its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell, which can kill.
**Fire:** keep fabric, paper patterns and fuel away from the iron and any heat source. Keep a fire extinguisher or a bucket of sand where you can reach it and know how to use it.
**Needles and blades:** keep fingers clear of the needle, change bent needles at once, store pins in a cushion and keep scissors closed when not in use.
**Body:** work in good light, take short breaks to stretch your back, neck and eyes, and keep the floor clear of offcuts to prevent falls.
Clients' data is personal data

Measurements, phone numbers, addresses and photos of clients are personal information. Nigeria's **Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how businesses handle personal data. In practice: keep your order book where others cannot read it, do not share a client's measurements or number with anyone else, and ask permission before posting a photo of a client wearing your work.
Worked example: a one-week setup plan
For example, Halima sews from a room in her house in Kaduna and wants to look and work more professionally before the next festive season.
Day 1: she sorts all client fabric into labelled bags and photographs each one with its tag.
Day 2: she replaces her stretched tape measure and frees one extension socket for the iron alone.
Day 3: she moves the generator outside, away from the window, and buys a small fire extinguisher.
Day 4: she searches two business names on the CAC portal and starts the registration form.
Day 5: she starts a new order book and sets up WhatsApp Business with her business statement.
In five days Halima reduces her risk of lost fabric, electrical fire and generator fumes, and starts her legal registration, all without renting a shop.

Late outfits, lost measurements and arguments over balances usually come from the same root: no fixed process. When every order goes through the same stages, and every stage leaves a written record, you can take more orders with less stress. This lesson gives you that process and the order book that holds it together.

Each stage ends with something written or photographed, so nothing depends on memory.
Stage by stage

**Consult.** Look at the style picture with the client, agree details (neckline, sleeve, length, lining, closures) and check that her fabric is enough. Write the style details and save the picture in her WhatsApp chat.

**Measure.** Take measurements with a good tape over light clothing and record them on her order page. For a women's gown this usually includes bust, under-bust, waist, hip, shoulder, bust point, half length (shoulder to waist), full length, sleeve length and round sleeve or arm.
**Deposit.** Agree the price and take a deposit that covers at least the materials you must buy. Issue a receipt with the order number, amount paid and balance.
**Cut and sew.** Schedule the order into a specific week. Pre-wash cotton fabrics such as some Ankara if the client agrees, because untreated cotton can shrink after the first wash.
**Fitting.** Invite the client for a try-on before final finishing. Note every adjustment on her page and agree a new date if needed.
**Finish and collect.** Press, check against your quality checklist, photograph the finished piece, collect the balance and only then release the garment.

Measurements are the part most likely to go wrong. Measure in the same order every time so you never skip one, keep the tape snug but not tight, and read it at eye level. Write the date beside every set, because bodies change: re-measure a returning client if it has been several months or she tells you her size has changed. If an apprentice takes measurements, check two or three of them yourself before cutting.

Setting due dates you can keep

Your **capacity** is how many garments you can finish in a week. Count real sewing hours, not hours in the shop. If you sew about 30 hours a week and an average gown takes about 8 hours, your capacity is about 3 to 4 gowns a week. Before you promise a date, look at what is already booked in that week.
Worked example: can she accept this order?
For example, Funmi sews about 30 hours a week in her Ibadan shop. A client asks on Monday for a lined gown by Saturday of next week.
Funmi checks her order book: this week has 3 gowns (about 24 hours) and next week has 2 gowns and a skirt suit (about 16 plus 10 hours).
This week is nearly full (24 of 30 hours). Next week has 26 of 30 hours booked, leaving about 4 hours.
The new gown needs about 8 hours, plus a fitting. It does not fit next week without overtime.
She offers two options: delivery in two weeks at the normal price, or next Saturday with an express charge that covers paid help from a trained helper.
The client chooses the two-week date. Funmi writes it in the book with a fitting date.
By checking capacity before saying yes, Funmi avoids a late delivery and offers an honest choice. The express option is priced to pay for the extra hands it needs.

Costing a garment and setting a profitable price
Cost a lined garment line by line: fabric, lining, trims, labour and overheads
Calculate an overhead rate per sewing hour from monthly running costs
Price both a full package (you supply fabric) and a sewing fee (client supplies fabric)
Decide when a price is too low to accept

In Nigeria, two kinds of price are common. With a **sewing fee** (also called workmanship), the client brings her fabric and you charge for making it. With a **full package**, you supply the fabric and everything else. You need to cost both correctly. The method is the same: add materials, labour and overheads, then add profit using the margin method from Module 1.
A spool of thread
Even small items like thread, zips and interfacing belong in the cost of every garment.
Step 1: Find your overhead rate
List your monthly running costs and divide by the sewing hours you work in a month. This gives an **overhead rate per hour** that you add to every garment according to how long it takes.
Monthly overhead (approximate)
Naira
Shop rent (yearly rent divided by 12)
Fuel and electricity
Data and phone
Needles, machine oil, servicing
Transport to market and deliveries
Total

If you sew about 200 hours a month (8 hours a day for 25 days), the overhead rate is 100,000 / 200 = **500 naira per hour**. If you sew fewer hours, the rate goes up, because the same rent and fuel are shared across fewer garments.
Step 2: Cost the garment
Worked example: full-package lined Ankara gown
For example, Zainab in Abuja makes a fitted, lined Ankara gown and supplies all materials. Prices below are approximate and vary by market and quality.
Fabric: one 6-yard piece of Ankara at about 15,000 naira.
Lining: 3 yards at about 1,000 naira per yard = 3,000 naira.
Trims: interfacing, invisible zip, thread and hooks = about 2,000 naira. Direct materials total = 20,000 naira.
Labour: 1 hour cutting, 5 hours sewing, 1 hour finishing and pressing, 1 hour for fitting = 8 hours x 1,000 naira = 8,000 naira.
Overheads: 8 hours x 500 naira = 4,000 naira.
Price for a 25% margin = 32,000 / 0.75 = 42,667 naira, rounded to 43,000 naira.
Zainab's full-package price is about 43,000 naira, giving roughly 11,000 naira profit on top of paying herself 8,000 naira for her labour. Anything below 32,000 naira loses money.
Worked example: the same gown as a sewing fee
For example, the next client brings her own Ankara and lining. Zainab supplies only the trims.
Trims: 2,000 naira.
Labour: 8,000 naira. Overheads: 4,000 naira.
Total cost = 14,000 naira.
Price for a 25% margin = 14,000 / 0.75 = 18,667, rounded to 19,000 naira.

Her sewing fee for this style is about 19,000 naira. If the shop next door charges 12,000 naira, Zainab now knows she cannot match that without losing money, so she competes on fit and finish instead.

Step 3: Check your price against the market

After costing, compare your price with three or four tailors who serve the same customer. If your price is much higher, look for waste before you cut your margin: are you buying lining in small pieces at a high price instead of by the roll? Are you losing hours to rework because of measuring mistakes? Is your overhead rate high because you sew few hours while paying for a large shop? If your price is much lower than theirs, you may be undercharging for good work, and you can raise it gradually as your portfolio grows.

When a client asks you to reduce your price, change the order rather than your margin. Offer a simpler style, no lining, fewer embellishments or a longer turnaround. That way the price comes down because the cost came down, and you still earn on every garment.
Pricing decisions that protect you
**Group orders:** cost one outfit, then check whether bulk fabric buying lowers material cost. Do not discount labour unless the styles are identical and faster to repeat.
**Express orders:** add a charge that pays for overtime or a helper.
**Complex styles:** heavy beading, corsets and stone work can take several times longer than a plain gown. Time yourself once and cost from real hours.

**Rising fabric prices:** fabric prices change often, so date your price list and review it regularly. For full-package orders, quote fabric at today's price and buy it as soon as the deposit arrives.
**Floor price:** your total cost is the lowest price you can accept. Below that, every order makes you poorer.

Bookkeeping simply means writing down every naira that comes in or goes out of the business, the same day. It does not need accounting training. It answers three questions every owner should be able to answer at any time: How much money does the business have? Who still owes me? Did I make a profit last month?
An open ledger book
A simple cash book, filled in daily, is the most useful financial tool a small fashion business can have.
Separate the money first

Open a separate account for the business: a business account in your registered business name, or at least a separate personal account used only for the shop. Ask clients to pay deposits and balances into it by transfer or POS. Pay yourself a fixed amount from it each week or month as your wage, and move it to your personal account. This one habit makes bookkeeping far easier, because your bank statement becomes a second record of business money.
Choosing your deposit level

Set your deposit so that, if a client disappears, you have not lost money. For full-package orders, the deposit should at least cover the fabric, lining and trims you will buy, because you cannot resell fabric cut to one person's size. For sewing-fee orders where the client brings fabric, many tailors ask for half or more before cutting. For large group orders, such as aso-ebi for a wedding, ask for deposits on every outfit before buying in bulk, and set a firm last date for measurements so you have time to sew. Write your deposit rule into your terms and apply it to everyone, including friends and church members.

In fashion, one badly fitted outfit at a wedding is seen by hundreds of guests, and the story travels faster than any advert. Quality is not only neat stitching. For your client it means three things: **it fits**, **it is well finished**, and **it is ready when promised**. This lesson shows how to protect all three with simple checks.

Hang the garment, turn it inside out and look at every seam. Try every zip and hook. Measure key points (bust, waist, length) against the order page. Remove all chalk marks and loose threads, then press. Photograph it front and back. If an apprentice did the work, the owner or senior tailor does this check, not the person who sewed it.
Why the fitting matters so much

Skipping the fitting to save time is the most expensive shortcut in tailoring. At a fitting, the garment is sewn but not finished: side seams can still be taken in or let out, the hem is not yet sewn, and sleeves can be adjusted. After finishing, the same change means unpicking overlocked seams and pressed hems, which takes longer and can leave marks. Book the fitting when you take the deposit, so the client plans for it. If a client cannot come, ask her to send a well-fitting garment of her own, and compare its measurements with your work.

Also check fabric before you cut. Look for flaws, holes or printing faults along the whole length, and show the client any you find. Lay the pattern so motifs line up at the centre front and across seams where the style needs it, and confirm she has enough fabric for her chosen style before cutting the first piece.

Listen fully and ask her to show you where it does not fit. Do not argue in front of others.

If it is your error, adjust it free and give a new date. If it is a new request outside the agreed style, explain the cost of the change politely.

Each slot needs a deposit to be confirmed; she does not 'hold' slots for promises.
She schedules fittings at least four days before each due date.
She closes bookings at 20 slots, keeping one slot free for an adjustment or emergency.
Ronke delivers all December orders on time, with fittings done. She turns away some work, but repeat clients return in January because they trust her dates.
Keep one spare slot
Always leave a little unbooked time in each week. Power cuts, illness and machine breakdowns happen, and spare time stops one problem from making every order late.

For example: one free adjustment within 7 days of collection if the fit does not match the agreed measurements; changes to style after cutting are charged; garments altered elsewhere are not covered. Send it with your order terms, so there are no surprises.

Apprenticeship is how many Nigerian tailors learned the trade, and how many shops grow. A good apprentice can take simple work off your hands within months. A badly managed arrangement brings wasted fabric, disputes with families and a bad name in the community. This lesson shows how to run it professionally and fairly.
A woman teaching a learner beside a board

Put the agreement in writing

In many places, apprenticeship terms are agreed by word of mouth, and that is where disputes start. Write a one-page agreement, read it aloud with the apprentice and a parent or guardian where relevant, and let each side keep a copy. It should cover:
**Duration:** how long the training lasts and what she should be able to do at the end.
**Fees:** any training fee, how and when it is paid, and whether it includes tools.
**Hours:** working days and times, and breaks.
**Stipend or pay:** whether she earns anything, for example once she can sew garments for clients.
**Tools and materials:** what she must bring and what the shop provides.
**Conduct and safety rules:** punctuality, care of clients' fabric, phone use, safety.
**Completion:** how her skills will be assessed and how the end of training (often called 'freedom') will be marked.

Start on offcuts, not client fabric. Give one clear task per stage and check it. Keep a simple skills record for each apprentice with the date each skill was signed off. This record protects you if a family asks why she is not yet sewing for clients, and it gives her a sense of progress.
Fair treatment and safety
Speak to apprentices with respect. Correct mistakes privately and show the right way. Beating, insults and threats are abuse and have no place in a professional workshop.
Teach safety on day one: needles, scissors, the iron, electrical sockets and keeping the generator outside.
Do not keep a school-age child away from school to work in the shop. Check that young people are of working age, involve parents or guardians, and follow your state's child-protection laws.
Do not hold an apprentice's documents or wages as a threat.
Provide water, toilet access and reasonable working hours.
Close supervision on machines and irons

New learners should use the iron and electric machines only under supervision until they show they can work safely. Show where the main switch and fire extinguisher are, and what to do if a socket sparks: switch off at the main and do not touch the appliance.
Handling problems with an apprentice

When problems come up, such as lateness, careless work or damaged fabric, deal with them early and calmly. Talk privately, describe the problem with a specific example, and agree what must change and by when. Write a short note of the conversation in her record. If the problem continues, involve her parent or guardian, or the person who introduced her, before it grows into a dispute. Ending an arrangement should follow what the written agreement says.
Paying helpers: per piece or fixed wage

Once a trained helper sews for clients, you can pay a **fixed wage** (weekly or monthly) or **per piece** (a set amount for each finished garment). Per-piece pay rewards speed and suits busy seasons, but you must check quality closely. A fixed wage suits steady work and encourages care, but you must keep enough orders flowing to cover it. Whichever you choose, include the cost in your labour rate when you price.

Grace offers Uche 5,000 naira per gown sewn to standard, matching 5 of the 8 labour hours.
Uche sews 10 gowns in two weeks and earns 50,000 naira.
Grace checks every gown against the pre-delivery checklist; 1 needs rework, which Uche fixes before payment.
Grace's own share of labour (3 hours per gown) and the overheads stay in her price, so her margin is protected.
Per-piece pay matched to the labour already in the price lets Grace take more orders without cutting her profit, while quality checks keep standards up.
Respect clients' privacy too
Teach apprentices that client measurements, phone numbers and photos stay in the shop. They should not post clients' outfits or contact clients privately without your permission.

Writing a one-page report
A report helps you think clearly, and it is useful if you apply for a loan or grant, join a cooperative, or explain the business to a partner. Keep it to one page with these parts:
**Headline:** one sentence on the month, for example 'More profit from fewer, better-planned orders.'
**Numbers:** the five key numbers for this month and last month side by side.
**What went well:** two or three points with evidence (a client review, an on-time rush).
**What went wrong:** honest points, such as a late order and why it happened.
**Action for next month:** one specific change and how you will measure it.
One action at a time

If you change everything at once, you cannot tell what worked. Pick the single change most likely to help, such as raising the price of one style or adding a fitting step, and see its effect in next month's numbers.
Reading what the numbers say
**Sales up, profit flat:** costs rose or prices are too low. Recheck your costing, especially fabric prices and overheads.
**On-time rate falling:** you are booking beyond capacity, or losing time to rework. Cap bookings and review your quality checklist.
**Repeat rate low:** clients are not coming back. Ask why: fit, finish, delays or price.
**Average order value rising:** you are selling higher-value work, such as lined or more detailed styles, or group orders. Good, as long as the on-time rate holds.
**Big balances owed:** profit on paper but no cash. Chase collections before taking new orders.

Keep the five numbers in a simple table, one column per month, at the back of your order book or in a spreadsheet. After three months you will see patterns that one busy week could never show you, such as which months are slow and when to run a promotion.

Taking good photos with a phone
**Light:** shoot in daylight near a window or outside in shade. Avoid harsh midday sun and the yellow light of indoor bulbs.
**Background:** a plain wall, curtain or sheet so the outfit stands out.

Clients rarely pay for stitches. They pay for how the outfit makes them look and feel at the event, for confidence that it will be ready on time, and for not having to worry. When you talk about your work in those terms, price becomes one part of the decision instead of the only part.

**Fit:** 'Made to your measurements, with a fitting before finishing.'

When a client says 'Please reduce it'

Bargaining is normal in Nigerian markets, so expect it and prepare. Never drop below your total cost. Instead, keep your price and add value, or keep your margin and reduce the cost of the order. Examples: 'I can do it at 35,000 without the lining' or 'For 40,000 you also get a matching headwrap.' For loyal clients, a small, planned discount (for example on a second outfit in the same order) can be fine if your costing still shows a profit.
Worked example: a church choir uniform proposal
For example, Blessing in Benin City is asked to quote for 30 choir gowns. Her costing sheet shows about 14,000 naira total cost per gown when the church supplies fabric. All figures are approximate.
She prices at a 20% margin for a bulk order: 14,000 / 0.8 = 17,500 naira per gown, total 525,000 naira.
She checks capacity: with one helper she can finish about 10 identical gowns a week, so she quotes 3 weeks from full measurements and deposit.
She asks for a 50% deposit (262,500 naira), the balance on delivery, and measurements of all 30 singers by a fixed date.
Her one-page proposal lists style, inclusions, price, deposit, timeline, fitting plan and alteration policy, with photos of similar work.
She sends it as a PDF on WhatsApp and follows up in three days.
The committee sees a clear, professional offer with dates they can plan around. Blessing's margin is protected even with the bulk price, because it starts from her real cost.

For uniform contracts with schools or companies, expect to be asked for your CAC certificate, a business account in the registered name and sometimes samples. Agree payment stages in writing before you buy anything, because some organisations pay only after delivery and you must not fund a large order from your own pocket without a deposit.
Taking payments safely

Common ways to receive payment include bank transfer to your business account, POS terminals from providers such as Moniepoint or OPay, and payment links from services such as Paystack, which let clients pay by card or transfer through a secure page. Whatever you use, the money must show in your account before a garment is released.
Payment scams to watch for

Fake credit alerts and edited screenshots: confirm in your banking app. 'Overpayment' tricks, where someone sends too much and asks for a refund, then the original payment is reversed: wait until it clears and refund only to the same account. Never share your PIN, password or OTP, and no real bank or payment company will ask for them by phone or chat.

Speed and tone in the first reply win many orders. Answer enquiries within a few hours during working days, greet the client by name, and give a direct answer before asking questions. For example: 'Good afternoon, Nkem. Thank you for your message. This style is from 22,000 naira with your fabric, ready in 10 days after measurement and deposit. When would you like to come for measurement?' Save versions of this as quick replies. If you cannot reply quickly, set an away message that says when you will respond.

Happy clients are your best marketing. After a good fitting, ask: 'Would you mind sending a short review I can share?' With permission, post it with a photo of the outfit. Business model
Bespoke or ready-to-wear?
Most Nigerian tailors start with bespoke work. The client brings fabric, you measure, she pays a deposit and collects later. It needs little stock, but your income depends on your hours.
Ready-to-wear can grow beyond your own hands, but your money is tied up in stock until it sells.
Many small brands mix the two: bespoke pays the bills while a small ready-to-wear line builds the brand.

Three parts of every garment's cost
Fabric, lining, interfacing, zip, buttons, thread, hooks for this one garment.
Your hours have a value. 150,000 naira wage over 150 hours is 1,000 naira an hour.
Rent, fuel, electricity, data, needles, machine servicing. Paid monthly, but real.
Total cost has three parts. First, direct materials: everything that goes into this one garment.
Second, labour, the most forgotten cost. If you want about 150,000 naira as your wage and you sew about 150 hours a month, your rate is 1,000 naira an hour.
A gown that takes 8 hours carries 8,000 naira of labour. If you skip it, you are working for free.
Third, overheads. Fuel, shop rent and data are costs of every garment, even though you pay them monthly.

For example, Bisi prices a lined Ankara gown.
Naira prices are approximate. Total is profit.
Now two words that confuse many tailors. Markup compares profit with cost. Margin compares profit with the selling price.
Bisi sells a lined Ankara gown for 40,000 naira. Her total cost is about 30,000.
Her profit is 10,000 naira. That is a 33% markup, but a 25% margin.
If she wrongly adds 25% to cost, she charges only 37,500 and her margin falls to 20%. To reach a 25% margin, divide the cost by 0.75.

Prevent mistakes
Common problems and their cure
Too tight or loose

Most problems have a simple cause. Wrong or old measurements. Cotton not pre-washed. Wrong tension or a blunt needle. Too many orders accepted.
So measure in a fixed order and date it. Offer to pre-wash cotton such as some Ankara. Test stitch on an offcut and press each seam.
And never skip the fitting. Before finishing, a seam is easy to adjust. After overlocking and pressing, the same change takes longer and can leave marks.
Every garment
Turn the garment inside out and look at every seam. Try every zip and hook. Measure the bust, waist and length against the order page, then press and photograph it.

Running apprenticeship fairly
A one-page agreement: duration, fees, hours, pay, tools, rules and completion.
Offcuts first, never client fabric. Sign off each skill with a date.
No beating or insults. Supervise the iron and machines. Never keep a child from school.
Many disputes start with word-of-mouth terms. Write a one-page agreement, read it aloud with the apprentice and a parent or guardian, and give each side a copy.
Start her on offcuts and keep a skills record with dates. It shows her progress and protects you.
Beating, insults and threats are abuse and have no place in a workshop. Teach safety on day one. New learners use the iron and machines only under supervision.
